passage:
Counsellor's note. Pranav came to see me after class, quiet and pale. Pranav said an online preacher tells followers that families who "cling" are chains, and asks each follower for a monthly donation from pocket money, and to say nothing to parents. Pranav said, "I feel guilty when I don't send it, and scared something bad will happen." Pranav had stopped eating with the cousins and felt lonely. I explained calmly that real guidance does not ask for secrecy, money or distance from family. I asked if we could tell Pranav's parents together. After a long silence Pranav agreed. I phoned Pranav's mother that afternoon.
- Vidya, school counsellor

qa.q: What did the preacher ask Pranav to keep from the parents?
qa.a: The preacher asked Pranav to say nothing to the parents about the monthly donation.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling, and what showed it?
qa.a: Pranav felt guilty, scared and lonely; the fear that something bad would happen if the money was not sent and the stopped meals with the cousins show it.

qa.q: What did Vidya do to help, and why does it work?
qa.a: Vidya explained that guidance which demands secrecy, money or distance is not real guidance, and brought in the parents, so a trusted adult can help. 🤍

qa.q: How might Pranav's parents feel on hearing this?
qa.a: Probably worried, but also relieved that Pranav told someone; the note only says that Vidya phoned Pranav's mother.

grounding: A preacher uses guilt, fear and secrecy to get Pranav's money and distance from family; a counsellor helps Pranav recognise it and involve parents.

passage:
"Why are you skipping the canteen again?" Sahil asked as they walked into Karthik's house after school.

"Saving my pocket money. For the mission."

"The guy in the videos?"

Karthik lowered his voice. "He says my family is spiritually asleep. That's why I feel so bad at home. If I give an offering and keep it between me and him, I'll be free. He sends me messages at night."

Sahil stopped in the hallway. "He's messaging you? And telling you to keep secrets from your family?"

"He said they wouldn't understand."

"Karthik, that's exactly what people say when they want you alone. Real teachers don't need your pocket money or your secrets."

Karthik felt his throat tighten. "I feel guilty just saying this out loud."

"Then say it to your Amma. Now. I'll stay."

They went into the kitchen. Karthik showed his mother the messages. She read them, set down her spoon and said, "I'm glad you told me. We'll block him together and report the account tonight."

qa.q: What was Karthik saving his pocket money for?
qa.a: Karthik was saving it for "the mission", as an offering.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling as he told Sahil about the messages?
qa.a: Karthik felt guilty and anxious, with his throat tightening, as if speaking up was a betrayal of the preacher.

qa.q: What warning signs did Sahil point out?
qa.a: Sahil pointed out that the preacher wanted money, secrecy from family and messages at night, which are ways of isolating someone.

qa.q: How did Karthik's Amma respond, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She thanked him for telling her and said they would block and report the account that night, which made Karthik feel safe rather than blamed.

grounding: It shows a teen targeted by a preacher who uses guilt and us-versus-them to get money and secrecy, recognising the signs and telling a trusted adult who acts the same day.

passage:
Looking back, the scariest thing is how normal it felt. I'm Joseph, and in Class 9 I found a preacher's channel that seemed to explain why I felt so alone. He said most people, even families, were "blind." Only his followers could see.

Then came the private group. Every night he posted things like, "If your family mocks your faith, they are not your real family." He asked for "seed offerings." He said, "What we share here stays here."

I sent him my birthday money. I stopped eating dinner with my parents because he said they would pull me down. I felt guilty all the time, guilty at home, guilty in the group.

My elder sister Jaya noticed I'd stopped laughing. She found me crying on the stairs and asked, very gently, what was going on. I showed her the group.

She sat with me, then took me straight to our mother. Amma read it all that evening, held my hand and said, "None of this is your fault." We reported the group together that night.

qa.q: What did the preacher call the money he asked for?
What was Joseph feeling during the months in the group?
qa.a: Joseph felt lonely and constantly guilty, both at home and in the group.

qa.q: What warning signs of manipulation are in the preacher's messages?
qa.a: He asked for money, demanded secrecy, and told Joseph the family at home was not a real family, which isolates and controls someone.

qa.q: How did Jaya help Joseph, and why did that matter?
qa.a: Jaya noticed Joseph had stopped laughing, asked gently and took Joseph to their mother that evening, so a trusted adult could step in the same day.

grounding: It shows a teen targeted by a preacher who uses guilt and us-versus-them to get money and cut off family, recognising it and telling a trusted adult.
